ety.text: From the short past participle of stancare (“to tire out”) in Tuscan; compare the Standard Italian participle stancato.

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese canssado, past participle of canssar (modern Portuguese cansar).

From Middle English tiren, tirien, teorien, from Old English tȳrian, tēorian (“to fail, cease, become weary, be tired, exhausted; tire, weary, exhaust”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-West Germanic *teuʀōn (“to cease”), which is possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dews- (“to fail, be behind, lag”). Compare Ancient Greek δεύομαι (deúomai, “to lack”), Sanskrit दोष (dóṣa, “crime, fault, vice, deficiency”).
Probably from Middle English tir(e) (“equipment, furnshings, ornament”). See the details at tyre.
From Middle English tire, from Old French tirer (“to draw or pull”), akin to English tear (“to rend”).

senses.d: US and Canada spelling of tyre: The rubber covering on a wheel.
A child's apron covering the upper part of the body, and tied with tape or cord; a pinafore. Also tier.

ex: men like apes follow the fashions in tires, gestures, actions: if the king laugh, all laugh […].
Ne spared they to strip her naked all. / Then when they had despoild her tire and call, / Such as she was, their eyes might her behold.

senses.d: A covering for the head; a headdress.
ex: And on her head she wore a tyre of gold,
[Jezebel] painted her face, and tired her head.

senses.d: To seize, pull, and tear prey, as a hawk does.
ex: Even as an empty eagle, sharp by fast, / Tires with her beak on feathers, flesh, and bone.
I grieve myself / To think, when thou shalt be disedged by her / That now thou tirest on, how thy memory / Will then be pang'd by me.

senses.d: To seize, rend, or tear something as prey; to be fixed upon, or engaged with, anything.
ex:
and now doth gaſtly death
With greedie talients gripe my bleeding hart,
And like a Harpye tires on my life.
Thus made she her remove, / And left wrath tyring on her son.
In posture to displode their second tire / Of thunder.
